kids.text: Electrostatics
Study of forces, fields and potentials from static charges
Static: does not move or change with time
Electric Charge
Discovery: Thales of Miletus, 600 BC (amber rubbed with wool)
Two types: Positive and Negative (named by Benjamin Franklin)
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract
Charge by rubbing: electrons transferred, no new charge created
Detection: Gold-leaf electroscope
Basic Properties
Additivity: total charge = algebraic sum of all charges
Conservation: total charge of isolated system is constant
Quantisation: q = ne, where n is integer, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C
Conductors and Insulators
Conductors: allow charge to flow freely (metals, human body, earth)
Insulators: resist charge flow (glass, plastic, rubber, wood)
Semiconductors: intermediate resistance (third category)
Charge on conductor spreads over entire surface
Charge on insulator stays at the point of application
Methods of Charging
Friction (triboelectric): rubbing transfers electrons
Conduction: direct contact with charged body
Induction: charged body brought near without contact
Coulomb's Law
F = k·q₁q₂ / r²  (force between two point charges)
k = 1/4πε₀ = 9×10⁹ Nm²/C²
ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² C²/Nm² (permittivity of free space)
Vector form: F₂₁ = −F₁₂ (Newton's third law)
Acts along the line joining charges
Valid for point charges at rest
In medium: F = kq₁q₂ / εᵣr²  (εᵣ = relative permittivity)
Forces Between Multiple Charges
Superposition principle: net force = vector sum of individual forces
F = F₁₂ + F₁₃ + F₁₄ + … (forces are independent)
Electric Field
E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge)
Unit: N/C or V/m
Vector quantity; direction = direction of force on +ve charge
Due to point charge: E = kq/r²
Electric Field Lines
Start from positive charges; end at negative charges
Tangent at any point gives direction of E
Closer lines → stronger field
Never cross each other
Cannot form closed loops in electrostatics
Electric Flux
Φ = E · A = EA cosθ
Scalar quantity; unit: Nm²/C
Represents number of field lines crossing a surface
Electric Dipole
Two equal and opposite charges (+q, −q) separated by distance 2a
Dipole moment: p = q × 2a (vector, from –q to +q)
Field on axial line: E = 2kp/r³ (along p)
Field on equatorial line: E = kp/r³ (opposite to p)
Torque in uniform field: τ = p × E = pE sinθ
Net force on dipole in uniform field = 0
Continuous Charge Distribution
Linear charge density: λ = dq/dl (C/m)
Surface charge density: σ = dq/dA (C/m²)
Volume charge density: ρ = dq/dV (C/m³)
Gauss's Law
Φ = q(enclosed) / ε₀ (total flux through closed surface)
Applies to any closed (Gaussian) surface
Simplifies symmetric field problems
Applications
Infinite line charge: E = λ/2πε₀r
Infinite plane sheet: E = σ/2ε₀
Uniformly charged spherical shell: E = kq/r² (outside); E = 0 (inside)
Electrostatic Potential
V = W/q (work done per unit positive charge)
Scalar quantity; unit: Volt (J/C)
Potential due to point charge: V = kq/r
Potential is zero at infinity (reference point)
Potential due to dipole: V = kp cosθ / r²
Potential due to system of charges: V = Σ kqᵢ/rᵢ (superposition)
Equipotential Surfaces
Surface where V is same at every point
No work done moving a charge along equipotential surface
Always perpendicular to electric field lines
For point charge: concentric spheres
For uniform field: parallel planes
Relation: E = −dV/dr (field is negative potential gradient)
Potential Energy
U = kq₁q₂/r (two-charge system)
Work done = Change in potential energy
Potential energy of system of charges: U = Σ kqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ (sum over pairs)
Potential Energy in External Field
Single charge: U = qV
Two charges in field: U = q₁V(r₁) + q₂V(r₂) + kq₁q₂/r₁₂
Dipole in field: U = −p·E = −pE cosθ
Electrostatics of Conductors
Electric field inside conductor = 0 (static situation)
Field at surface is perpendicular to the surface
No excess charge inside conductor; all charge resides on surface
Entire conductor (and surface) is at same potential
Field at surface: E = σ/ε₀
Electrostatic shielding: field inside hollow conductor is zero
Dielectrics and Polarisation
Dielectrics: insulators that can be polarised by external field
Polar dielectrics: molecules have permanent dipole moment (e.g. water)
Non-polar dielectrics: dipole moment induced by external field
Polarisation P = χₑ ε₀ E (χₑ = electric susceptibility)
Dielectric constant K = ε/ε₀ (reduces effective field inside)
Capacitance
C = Q/V (charge stored per unit potential)
Unit: Farad (F) = C/V
Parallel plate capacitor: C = ε₀A/d
With dielectric: C = Kε₀A/d (K times greater)
Combination of Capacitors
Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + … (same charge, voltage divides)
Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ + … (same voltage, charge adds)
Energy Stored in Capacitor
U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV
Energy density: u = ½ε₀E²
Electric Current
I = dQ/dt (rate of flow of charge)
Unit: Ampere (A); scalar quantity
Conventional current: direction of +ve charge flow
Electron flow opposite to conventional current direction
Ohm's Law
V = IR (voltage = current × resistance)
Resistance R = ρl/A (ρ = resistivity, l = length, A = area)
Ohmic materials: linear V-I graph
Current density: j = I/A = σE (σ = conductivity = 1/ρ)
Limitations of Ohm's Law
Non-linear V-I in semiconductors and diodes
Asymmetric response for current reversal (e.g. electrolyte)
V not single-valued function of I in some devices
Drift of Electrons and Resistivity
Thermal velocity of electrons: random, no net direction
Drift velocity vd = eEτ/m (τ = relaxation time)
Resistivity: ρ = m/ne²τ
Mobility: μ = |vd|/E = eτ/m (unit: m²/Vs)
Resistivity of Materials
Metals: low resistivity (10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ωm)
Insulators: high resistivity (10¹⁰ to 10¹⁷ Ωm)
Semiconductors: intermediate, decreases with temperature
Temperature dependence: ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]
Nichrome/Manganin: very weak temperature dependence (used in standard resistors)
Electrical Energy and Power
Power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R
Energy dissipated (Joule heating): W = Pt = I²Rt
Power transmission: low current → low loss (P_loss = I²Rc)
Cells, EMF and Internal Resistance
EMF (ε): potential difference across cell when no current flows
Terminal voltage: V = ε − Ir (during discharge)
Internal resistance r reduces effective voltage
Cells in Combination
Series: ε_total = ε₁+ε₂, r_total = r₁+r₂ (for same EMF)
Parallel: same EMF cells; r_eff = r/n; useful for large current
Kirchhoff's Rules
Junction Rule (KCL): ΣI = 0 at any junction (charge conservation)
Loop Rule (KVL): ΣV = 0 around any closed loop (energy conservation)
Wheatstone Bridge
Balance condition: P/Q = R/S (no current through galvanometer)
Used to measure unknown resistance accurately
Meter Bridge: practical form of Wheatstone bridge
Potentiometer: measures EMF and internal resistance without drawing current
Magnetic Force
Lorentz force: F = q(E + v×B)
Magnetic force on moving charge: F = qv×B
Force ⊥ to both v and B; does no work
Force on current-carrying conductor: F = Il×B
Motion in Magnetic Field
Circular motion: r = mv/qB (radius of circular path)
Time period: T = 2πm/qB (independent of velocity)
Cyclotron frequency: ν = qB/2πm
Helical path: when v has component along B
Cyclotron
Accelerates charged particles using alternating electric field
Uses magnetic field to curve path in D-shaped chambers (dees)
Limitation: fails at relativistic speeds
Biot-Savart Law
dB = (μ₀/4π) Idl×r̂ / r²
μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ Tm/A (permeability of free space)
Direction: right-hand rule (curl fingers along current, thumb = B)
Field at centre of circular loop: B = μ₀I/2R
Field on axis of circular loop: B = μ₀IR²/2(R²+x²)^(3/2)
Ampere's Circuital Law
∮B·dl = μ₀I_enclosed
Analogous to Gauss's Law for magnetism
Field inside solenoid: B = μ₀nI (n = turns per unit length)
Field inside toroid: B = μ₀NI/2πr
Force Between Parallel Currents
Parallel currents attract; anti-parallel currents repel
Force per unit length: F/l = μ₀I₁I₂/2πd
Definition of Ampere based on this force
Torque on Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
Torque: τ = m×B = NIA sinθ (m = magnetic moment)
Magnetic moment: m = NIA (N=turns, I=current, A=area)
Loop acts like a magnetic dipole
Potential energy: U = −m·B
Moving Coil Galvanometer
Works on torque on current loop in magnetic field
Deflection: θ = NBAk I (k = spring constant)
Converted to Ammeter: add low resistance shunt in parallel
Converted to Voltmeter: add high resistance in series
Bar Magnet
Has north and south poles; always exists as dipole
Magnetic field lines: closed loops from N to S outside, S to N inside
Axial field: B = μ₀/4π · 2m/r³
Equatorial field: B = μ₀/4π · m/r³ (opposite to m)
Torque in uniform field: τ = m×B
Potential energy: U = −mB cosθ
Current loop analogy: m = IA (current loop = equivalent bar magnet)
Earth's Magnetism
Earth behaves like a huge bar magnet (geographic S pole near magnetic N)
Magnetic declination: angle between geographic and magnetic north
Magnetic dip (inclination): angle B makes with horizontal
Horizontal component: BH = B cosδ; Vertical: BV = B sinδ
Magnetism and Gauss's Law
∮B·dA = 0 (no magnetic monopoles exist)
Magnetic field lines are always closed loops
Magnetisation and Magnetic Intensity
Magnetisation M = net magnetic moment per unit volume
Magnetic intensity H: B = μ₀(H + M)
Susceptibility: χm = M/H
Relative permeability: μr = 1 + χm
Magnetic Properties of Materials
Diamagnetic
χm small and negative (e.g. copper, bismuth, water)
Weakly repelled by magnets
No permanent dipole moment; induced moment opposes field
Paramagnetic
χm small and positive (e.g. aluminium, platinum)
Weakly attracted by magnets
Curie's Law: χm = C/T
Ferromagnetic
χm large and positive (e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt)
Strongly attracted; can be permanently magnetised
Domains: regions of aligned magnetic moments
Curie temperature: above it, ferromagnetic → paramagnetic
Hysteresis: lag between B and H; area = energy lost per cycle
Faraday's and Henry's Experiments
Changing magnetic flux through a coil induces EMF
EMF induced when magnet moved relative to coil
Changing current in one coil induces EMF in adjacent coil
Magnetic Flux
Φ = B·A = BA cosθ
Unit: Weber (Wb); 1 Wb = 1 Vs
Faraday's Law of Induction
ε = −dΦ/dt (induced EMF = rate of change of flux)
For N turns: ε = −N dΦ/dt
Lenz's Law
Induced current opposes the change in flux causing it
Consequence of conservation of energy
Gives the direction of induced current (negative sign in Faraday's law)
Motional EMF
ε = Blv (conductor of length l moving with velocity v in field B)
Force on charges due to magnetic field drives current
Eddy currents: induced in solid conductors (used in braking, heating)
Inductance
Self Inductance
Φ = LI; L = self-inductance (Henry, H)
ε = −L dI/dt (back EMF opposes change in current)
Solenoid: L = μ₀n²Al
Mutual Inductance
Φ₂₁ = MI₁; M = mutual inductance
ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt
Two coaxial solenoids: M = μ₀n₁n₂Al
AC Generator
Rotating coil in magnetic field generates sinusoidal EMF
ε = NBAω sinωt = ε₀ sinωt
Parts: armature coil, field magnet, slip rings, brushes
AC Basics
v = V₀ sinωt; i = I₀ sinωt
RMS values: Vrms = V₀/√2; Irms = I₀/√2
Phasor: rotating vector representing sinusoidal quantities
AC Circuits
Pure Resistor
V and I in phase; P = Vrms·Irms
Pure Inductor
I lags V by 90°
Inductive reactance: XL = ωL
No power consumed (ideal inductor)
Pure Capacitor
I leads V by 90°
Capacitive reactance: XC = 1/ωC
No power consumed (ideal capacitor)
Series LCR Circuit
Impedance: Z = √(R² + (XL−XC)²)
Phase angle: tanφ = (XL−XC)/R
Resonance: XL = XC → Z = R (minimum impedance)
Resonant frequency: ω₀ = 1/√(LC)
Q-factor = ω₀L/R (sharpness of resonance)
Power in AC Circuit
P = Vrms·Irms·cosφ (cosφ = power factor)
Resistive circuit: P = I²rms·R (power factor = 1)
Pure L or C: P = 0 (power factor = 0)
Wattless current: component that contributes no power
Transformers
Works on mutual induction principle
V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ (turns ratio)
Step-up: N₂>N₁ (increases voltage, decreases current)
Step-down: N₂<N₁ (decreases voltage, increases current)
Ideal: P_in = P_out (100% efficiency)
Energy losses: eddy currents, flux leakage, hysteresis, resistance
Displacement Current
Id = ε₀ dΦE/dt (Maxwell's modification to Ampere's law)
Exists between capacitor plates during charging/discharging
Modified Ampere's Law: ∮B·dl = μ₀(Ic + Id)
Electromagnetic Waves
Produced by accelerating charges
E and B are mutually perpendicular and ⊥ to direction of propagation
Speed in vacuum: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3×10⁸ m/s
E₀/B₀ = c (ratio of field amplitudes)
Transverse waves; carry energy and momentum
Intensity: I = ½ε₀cE₀²
Maxwell's Equations (Summary)
∮E·dA = q/ε₀ (Gauss's Law for E)
∮B·dA = 0 (Gauss's Law for B; no monopoles)
∮E·dl = −dΦB/dt (Faraday's Law)
∮B·dl = μ₀Ic + μ₀ε₀ dΦE/dt (Ampere-Maxwell Law)
Electromagnetic Spectrum
Radio waves: λ > 0.1m; AM/FM radio, TV
Microwaves: 1mm–0.1m; radar, microwave ovens, satellite links
Infrared: 700nm–1mm; heat, remote controls, night vision
Visible light: 400–700 nm; VIBGYOR (human eye detects)
Ultraviolet: 10–400nm; kills bacteria, causes sunburn
X-rays: 0.01–10nm; medical imaging, crystal diffraction
Gamma rays: λ < 0.01nm; from nuclear reactions, most energetic
Reflection by Spherical Mirrors
Laws of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Sign convention: distances measured from pole; +ve in direction of incident light
Focal length f = R/2 (R = radius of curvature)
Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Magnification: m = −v/u
Concave mirror: converging; used in headlights, solar concentrators
Convex mirror: diverging; wider field of view; used in rear-view mirrors
Refraction
Snell's Law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂
Refractive index n = c/v = sin(i)/sin(r)
Light bends towards normal when entering denser medium
Total Internal Reflection
Occurs when light travels from denser to rarer medium
Critical angle: sin(c) = n₂/n₁ (for angle ≥ c, all light reflected)
Applications: optical fibre, diamonds, mirage, prism binoculars
Optical fibres: TIR enables lossless light transmission over long distances
Refraction by Spherical Surfaces and Lenses
Refraction formula: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂−n₁)/R
Lens maker's equation: 1/f = (n−1)[1/R₁ − 1/R₂]
Thin lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
Power of lens: P = 1/f (dioptre, D)
Combination of lenses: 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂; P = P₁ + P₂
Convex (converging): real, inverted image (object beyond F)
Concave (diverging): virtual, erect, diminished image always
Refraction Through a Prism
Deviation: δ = (i₁ + i₂) − A
Minimum deviation: i₁ = i₂; ray passes symmetrically
n = sin[(A+Dm)/2] / sin(A/2)
Dispersion: splitting of white light into spectrum (VIBGYOR)
Violet deviates most; red deviates least
Optical Instruments
Simple Microscope
Magnifying power m = 1 + D/f (D = 25cm, least distance of distinct vision)
Compound Microscope
Objective: short focal length, forms real magnified image
Eyepiece: acts as simple magnifier
Total magnification m = m₀ × mₑ
Telescope (Refracting)
Objective: large focal length; eyepiece: short focal length
Magnification: m = f₀/fₑ (normal adjustment)
Reflecting telescope: uses concave mirror as objective (no chromatic aberration)
Huygens Principle
Every point on wavefront is source of secondary wavelets
New wavefront = common tangent to all secondary wavelets
Explains reflection, refraction, and diffraction of waves
Refraction and Reflection using Huygens Principle
Refraction: proves Snell's law (n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂)
Speed of light in medium: v = c/n
TIR: at critical angle, refracted ray grazes the surface
Coherence and Superposition
Coherent sources: same frequency and constant phase difference
Incoherent: random phase difference; no sustained interference
Constructive interference: path difference = nλ
Destructive interference: path difference = (2n+1)λ/2
Young's Double Slit Experiment
Two coherent sources from single source via two slits
Fringe width: β = λD/d (D=distance to screen, d=slit separation)
Bright fringe at y = nλD/d; dark fringe at y = (2n+1)λD/2d
Intensity: I = 4I₀ cos²(δ/2) (max = 4I₀, min = 0)
Diffraction
Bending of light around obstacles/edges
Single slit: central maximum, secondary maxima and minima
Condition for minima: a sinθ = nλ
Width of central maximum: 2λD/a
Limit of resolution: θ = 1.22λ/D (Rayleigh criterion)
Polarisation
Transverse waves can be polarised; longitudinal cannot
Plane polarised light: E oscillates in one plane only
Polaroids: selectively transmit light of one polarisation
Malus's Law: I = I₀ cos²θ
Brewster's angle: tanθ_B = n (reflected light is plane polarised)
Polarisation by scattering: sky appears blue (Rayleigh scattering)

chapters.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

data.text: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

kids.text: Electron Emission
Work function φ: minimum energy to free electron from metal
Thermionic emission: heating the metal
Field emission: strong electric field applied
Photoelectric emission: light of sufficient frequency
Photoelectric Effect
Hertz (1887): UV light causes spark discharge
Hallwachs: UV light on zinc plate causes negative charge loss
Threshold frequency ν₀: minimum frequency for photoelectric effect
Stopping potential Vs: voltage to stop most energetic photoelectrons
Effect is instantaneous; independent of intensity for threshold
Experimental Observations
Photocurrent ∝ intensity of light (for fixed frequency > ν₀)
Max KE depends on frequency, not intensity
Stopping potential ∝ frequency (Vs = h(ν−ν₀)/e)
Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
Light consists of photons, each with energy E = hν
KE_max = hν − φ = hν − hν₀
h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ Js (Planck's constant)
Wave theory fails to explain PE effect; quantum theory succeeds
Particle Nature of Light: The Photon
Photon: quantum of electromagnetic energy
Energy: E = hν = hc/λ
Momentum: p = h/λ = E/c
Rest mass = 0; always travels at speed c
Wave Nature of Matter (de Broglie)
de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/p = h/mv
Matter waves: every moving particle has an associated wave
For electron: λ = h/√(2meV) (accelerated through potential V)
Verified by Davisson-Germer experiment (electron diffraction)
Wave-particle duality: light and matter exhibit both properties
Alpha Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Model
Geiger-Marsden experiment: α-particles bombarded on gold foil
Most α-particles pass through; some deflected; very few bounce back
Rutherford's conclusion: nucleus is tiny, dense, positively charged
Distance of closest approach: d = kZe²/KE_α
Impact parameter: determines angle of scattering
Nuclear radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m; atomic radius ~10⁻¹⁰ m
Limitation: accelerating electrons should radiate and spiral in (unstable)
Atomic Spectra
Emission spectrum: discrete bright lines on dark background
Absorption spectrum: dark lines on continuous spectrum
Hydrogen series: Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen (IR), Brackett, Pfund
Rydberg formula: 1/λ = RH(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²); RH = 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹
Bohr's Model of Hydrogen Atom
Postulate 1: electrons move in certain stable circular orbits without radiation
Postulate 2: angular momentum quantised: mvr = nh/2π
Postulate 3: photon emitted/absorbed when electron jumps between orbits
Radius of nth orbit: rn = n²a₀ (a₀ = 0.529 Å, Bohr radius)
Energy of nth level: En = −13.6/n² eV
Ground state energy = −13.6 eV; ionisation energy = 13.6 eV
Photon energy: hν = En₂ − En₁ (transition energy)
de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Quantisation
Electron wave in orbit must form standing wave: 2πr = nλ
λ = h/mv → mvr = nh/2π (reproduces Bohr's condition)
Atomic Masses and Nuclear Composition
Nucleus: protons (Z) + neutrons (N); mass number A = Z + N
Isotopes: same Z, different A; isobars: same A, different Z
Atomic mass unit: 1u = 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV/c²
Proton mass: 1.00727 u; Neutron: 1.00866 u
Size of Nucleus
Nuclear density is constant (~2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³) for all nuclei
Mass-Energy and Binding Energy
Einstein: E = mc² (mass-energy equivalence)
Mass defect: Δm = [Zmp + Nmn] − M_nucleus
Binding energy: BE = Δm × c² = Δm × 931.5 MeV
BE per nucleon: peaks around Fe-56 (~8.8 MeV) → most stable
Light nuclei: fusion releases energy; heavy nuclei: fission releases energy
Nuclear Force
Strong nuclear force: short range (~few fm), charge-independent
Attractive for r > 0.8 fm; repulsive at very short range
Much stronger than Coulomb force at nuclear distances
Radioactivity
Spontaneous disintegration of unstable nuclei
Alpha (α) decay: emits ⁴He nucleus; A−4, Z−2
Beta (β⁻) decay: neutron → proton + electron + antineutrino
Gamma (γ) decay: high energy photon from excited nucleus
Decay law: N = N₀e^(−λt); half-life T½ = 0.693/λ
Activity: A = λN (unit: Becquerel; 1 Bq = 1 decay/s)
Nuclear Energy
Nuclear Fission
Heavy nucleus splits into smaller nuclei + energy
Example: ²³⁵U + n → ⁹²Kr + ¹⁴¹Ba + 3n + ~200 MeV
Chain reaction: controlled (reactor) or uncontrolled (bomb)
Critical mass: minimum mass for sustained chain reaction
Nuclear Fusion
Light nuclei fuse to form heavier nucleus + energy
Energy source of stars: H→He in sun (proton-proton cycle)
Requires very high temperature (~10⁷ K): thermonuclear fusion
Higher energy release per nucleon than fission
Classification of Solids
Conductors: overlapping valence and conduction bands
Insulators: large band gap (>3eV); electrons cannot cross
Semiconductors: small band gap (~1eV); e.g. Si (1.1eV), Ge (0.7eV)
Valence band: filled; Conduction band: empty at 0K
Intrinsic Semiconductor
Pure semiconductor; no impurity
At room temp: thermal energy breaks covalent bonds → electron-hole pairs
ni = number of electrons = number of holes
Conductivity increases with temperature (unlike metals)
Extrinsic Semiconductor
n-type
Doped with pentavalent impurity (P, As, Sb)
Electrons are majority carriers; holes are minority
Donor level just below conduction band
p-type
Doped with trivalent impurity (B, Al, In)
Holes are majority carriers; electrons are minority
Acceptor level just above valence band
p-n Junction
Formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductors
Depletion region: immobile ion charges near junction; no free carriers
Built-in potential barrier (contact potential) at junction
Biasing
Forward bias: reduces barrier, large current flows
Reverse bias: widens depletion layer, tiny reverse saturation current
I-V characteristics: exponential in forward bias; flat in reverse
Junction Diode as Rectifier
Half-Wave Rectifier
One diode; conducts only during positive half cycle
Output: pulsating DC; efficiency low
Full-Wave Rectifier
Two diodes + centre-tap transformer; or bridge rectifier (4 diodes)
Both half cycles utilised; smoother output
Filter (capacitor): smoothens pulsating DC to steady DC
Special Diodes
Zener diode: operates in reverse breakdown for voltage regulation
LED: forward-biased diode emits photons (E = hν = Eg)
Photodiode: reverse-biased; photocurrent ∝ light intensity
Solar cell: p-n junction converts solar energy to electrical energy
